title: The Truth About Airbnb Arbitrage and What I Do Now Instead
summary: Short-term rental operator compares Airbnb arbitrage with co-hosting: fixed rent and new competition turned a unit cash-flow negative, and arbitrage has no exit.

assertions.quote: the double-edged sword is you have more downside. And guys, the downside is real.

verdicts.note: A fixed lease obligation against variable revenue is the structural risk of the model.

assertions.quote: almost all of them did their best the first or second year and then leveled off afterwards. Meanwhile, the rent has only gone up.

verdicts.note: Consistent with rising short-term rental supply after 2022; based on one operator's portfolio.

assertions.quote: someone literally came down the road and rented an entire 18-unit apartment building

verdicts.note: Revenue per listing fell in many US markets as supply grew after 2022.

assertions.quote: there has been no legit mergers and acquisitions in the arbitrage space for almost a decade

verdicts.note: Lease-based operations have no transferable asset beyond furniture and lease assignment.

assertions.quote: even in a bullish case for arbitrage, I would have just made about the same had I just managed the property without any risk anyways

verdicts.note: Management fees of 20-30% are standard; arbitrage upside is higher in good markets, downside unbounded.

assertions.quote: rent was lower back then. And on average, properties just did better than they are doing today.

verdicts.note: Supply growth and rent increases since 2022 are documented, though some markets still work.

assertions.quote: I needed to put about $35,000 on a credit card.

verdicts.note: Empire had purchasers open business credit cards or loans for $15,000-$80,000 of working capital on top of the package fee, and many were left with credit-card debt they could not repay; the debt financed inventory rather than the course fee itself.
